references.text: Solomon's proverb that "a wound from a friend is faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful" (Prov 27:6). Judas' kiss was precisely an enemy's kiss disguised as friendship—a betrayal carried out through a sign of love.

Joab seized Amasa by the beard with his right hand as if to kiss him, but stabbed him in the stomach with his sword (2 Sam 20:9). A parallel example from the Old Testament where a kiss is used as a treacherous signal while the true intention is betrayal.
Absalom used false kisses and greetings to steal the people's hearts away from King David (2 Sam 15:5-6). An example of how a kiss can be used as an instrument of deceit and betrayal.

Matthew's parallel account of Judas' betraying kiss (Matt 26:48-50). Here more detail is given about the agreement with the chief priests that whoever Judas kissed was the one they should seize, and Jesus calls him "friend".
Mark's parallel account of Judas' betraying kiss (Mark 14:44-45). Judas had given them a prearranged signal: "The one I kiss is the man; seize him and lead him away under guard."
Earlier in Luke's account it is told that Satan entered Judas, and he went to the chief priests to arrange how he could betray Jesus (Luke 22:3-6). This agreement is now fulfilled with the kiss.

David's lament: "Even my close friend, someone I trusted, one who shared my bread, has turned against me" (Ps 41:10). A messianic prophecy about being betrayed by a close friend—fulfilled through Judas' kiss.
Jesus himself quotes Ps 41:10 and applies it to the one who will betray him: "He who shares my bread has lifted up his heel against me" (John 13:18). Jesus knew beforehand about Judas' betrayal.

Jesus' words at the Last Supper: "But see, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined" (Luke 22:21-22). Jesus foretold the betrayal by referring to the "Son of Man"—the same expression he uses in verse 48.

Daniel's vision of the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven and given power and glory (Dan 7:13-14). Jesus uses the title "Son of Man" for himself in Luke 22:48, a title with deep roots in this prophecy—and it underscores the contrast between his heavenly dignity and the humiliating treatment he suffers through betrayal.
